paragraphs.heading: A plain at the bottom of the sea
paragraphs.text: An abyssal plain is a plain under the sea, on the deep ocean floor, usually between 3,000 and 6,000 metres down. It generally stretches from the base of a continental rise out to a mid-ocean ridge. These plains are among the flattest and smoothest places on Earth. They are also among the least explored.

paragraphs.heading: New crust from the ridge
paragraphs.text: An abyssal plain begins with seafloor spreading, part of plate tectonics, and with melting of the lower oceanic crust. Magma rises from above the asthenosphere, which is a layer of the upper mantle. When this basaltic material reaches the surface at a mid-ocean ridge, it becomes new oceanic crust. Spreading of the seafloor keeps pulling that crust away to the sides.

paragraphs.heading: Smoothed over by mud
paragraphs.text: The fresh oceanic crust starts out with an uneven surface. Over time a blanket of fine sediment, mostly clay and silt, covers the bumps and makes the plain. Much of that sediment is carried by turbidity currents, which are funnelled from the edges of the continents down submarine canyons into deeper water. Most of the rest is pelagic sediment.

paragraphs.heading: What lies on the floor
paragraphs.text: In some areas of the plains, metallic nodules are common. They hold differing amounts of metals such as manganese, iron, nickel, cobalt and copper. Carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and silicon are found there as well, left by material that sinks down and breaks apart.

paragraphs.heading: Short of oxygen
paragraphs.text: The water over an abyssal plain is poor in oxygen, and animals there take in what dissolved oxygen there is. Much of that oxygen came from polar regions that melted long ago. Because oxygen is so scarce, the plains are a hard home for creatures that would thrive in the richer water above.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to find in old rocks
paragraphs.text: Abyssal plains were not recognized as their own kind of sea floor feature until the late 1940s. Until recently, none had been studied in a systematic way. Old plains are also rare in the sedimentary record, because subduction tends to swallow them.
